strengths: Addresses a relevant and practically motivated NLP-security problem: detecting compromised agents without labeled attack examples.
The hierarchical representation combines response semantics with local-neighborhood and system-level context in a simple, understandable architecture.

Evaluation spans three attack families, four communication topologies, several QA/security datasets, and three LLM backbones; results generally improve over the included unsupervised graph-anomaly baselines.
The paper evaluates both malicious-agent detection (AUROC) and downstream attack mitigation (ASR), and includes an informative ablation of neighborhood- and global-level features.
weaknesses: The central claim of safeguarding against unknown attacks is overstated. Evaluation covers only three preselected attack families whose responses are assumed to be semantic outliers; there are no adaptive, stealthy, coordinated-majority, or distribution-shift attacks that test this assumption.

Deployment requires selecting the top K=3 agents as malicious. This appears to provide prior knowledge of the attack budget, forces false positives when no or fewer agents are compromised, and is not varied. Benign-system utility, false-positive rates, threshold calibration, and robustness to different attacker prevalence are not reported.

The remediation description is internally inconsistent. Equation 8 filters edges using only one endpoint despite claiming bidirectional isolation, and Algorithm 1 uses another one-endpoint condition. Given the earlier directed-edge convention, neither clearly removes every incoming and outgoing edge incident to an anomalous node.

Experimental reporting is insufficient for reproducibility: the paper omits dataset/sample counts and splits, normal-training data construction, agent roles and counts in the main experiments, number and placement of attackers, attack prompts/configurations, SentenceBERT checkpoint, corruption fraction, alpha, temperature, epochs, seeds, and model-selection protocol. The stated code link is blank.

Reported numbers lack variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite stochastic LLM generation and training. It is also unclear whether baselines received comparable tuning and remediation budgets.

The evidence does not isolate whether the learned detector is necessary for downstream gains. Important controls are missing, including random top-K pruning, raw SentenceBERT similarity, simple one-class detectors, and ablations of corruption, contrastive training, and corruption intensity. The current ablation addresses only the hierarchical features.

The method assumes clean normal-only training data and strong semantic deviation by attackers, but neither training-set contamination nor camouflage is tested. The global-mean similarity score may be especially vulnerable when attackers form a coherent group or a large fraction of the system.

The supervised-contrastive objective in Equation 6 differs from the standard formulation by excluding other positive samples from the denominator, without justification. More generally, some mathematical notation and implementation details are inconsistent, weakening confidence that the method can be reproduced exactly.

The experiments are largely synthetic QA-style MAS configurations. Claims of practical, real-world, universal safeguarding would require more realistic agent workflows, clean-task utility measurements, and attack-specific safety outcomes such as unauthorized tool execution—not only answer-level ASR.

strengths: Addresses a relevant NLP security problem: defending LLM-based multi-agent systems without labeled malicious-agent examples.

The proposed pipeline is conceptually simple and computationally lightweight, combining frozen sentence embeddings, multi-level graph context, synthetic corruption, contrastive learning, and graph pruning.

Evaluation spans three attack modalities, four communication topologies, several task datasets, and three LLM backbones. The paper also reports detection AUC and downstream attack success rate rather than relying on detection alone.
The comparison with generic unsupervised graph-anomaly methods generally suggests that a detector tailored to multi-agent interactions can be beneficial.
weaknesses: The central claim of robust defense against unknown attacks is insufficiently supported. All evaluations use three anticipated attack families under a single experimental framework, with no adaptive, stealthy, transfer-across-dataset, or genuinely novel attack evaluation. The method fundamentally assumes that malicious responses are semantic outliers, an assumption that subtle attacks, role-dependent outputs, propagated misinformation, or a coordinated majority can violate.

The top-K remediation protocol appears to assume that exactly three agents should be removed. This supplies consequential information about attack prevalence and forces agents to be flagged even in a clean system. The paper provides no threshold-selection procedure, false-positive analysis, clean-system utility, or experiments varying the number and fraction of attackers.

The remediation formulation is internally inconsistent. Given the paper's convention that e_ij carries a message from v_j to v_i, Equation 8 filters only on v_i and therefore does not remove all incoming and outgoing edges incident to an anomalous agent, contrary to the claimed bidirectional isolation. The algorithm uses different indexing, leaving the implemented intervention unclear.

Evidence for the proposed design is incomplete. The only ablation removes neighborhood/global features; there are no ablations of synthetic corruption, contrastive learning versus a classifier, contextual scoring, or pruning. Sensitivity to corruption magnitude, corruption rate, temperature, anomaly budget, graph size, and attack prevalence is also absent. Simple non-graph anomaly baselines on frozen SentenceBERT features are needed to establish that the hierarchical encoder is responsible for the gains.

Several empirical claims overstate the tables. BlindGuard does not consistently outperform every unsupervised baseline in downstream ASR, its AUC can be near 60–70, and it remains far behind the supervised method in many settings. Calling its performance broadly comparable to the supervised upper bound is therefore misleading. The scalability table evaluates only BlindGuard and no defense, while the undefended ASR itself changes sharply with system size, so it does not establish scalability convincingly.

The experiments lack essential reproducibility information: training-set size and construction, train/test separation, default number and roles of agents, number of compromised agents, prompt and attack-generation details, sample counts, random seeds, repeated-run variation or confidence intervals, SentenceBERT checkpoint, MLP architecture, corruption rate and magnitude, temperature, epochs, model-selection protocol, and baseline tuning. The abstract's code-availability statement has no usable link in the manuscript.

The corruption scheme adds isotropic Gaussian noise directly to sentence embeddings, likely producing easily separable off-manifold vectors rather than realistic adversarial language. No analysis demonstrates that these pseudo-anomalies resemble real attacked-agent representations or explains why a detector trained on them should generalize. The contrastive-loss claim that this avoids overfitting to synthetic corruption is asserted rather than tested.

There are additional technical and presentation problems: Equation 1 is not a valid conventional classification loss as written; the inference score includes each node's self-similarity; the same global mean is appended to every node and can itself be contaminated; sample sizes and statistical uncertainty are absent; and multiple typographical or labeling errors reduce confidence. Overall, the idea is relevant but important methodological clarification and substantially stronger evaluation are required before the contribution is adequately sound and reproducible.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important NLP security problem: defending LLM-based multi-agent systems when labeled examples of malicious agents are unavailable.

BlindGuard is conceptually coherent and relatively simple, combining response embeddings, agent/neighborhood/system-level context, synthetic feature corruption, contrastive training, anomaly scoring, and graph remediation.

The empirical scope is broad in several useful respects: three attack modalities, six attack/dataset configurations, four communication topologies, multiple LLM backbones, and a limited scaling experiment with 20 and 50 agents.

The reported results generally show stronger detection and downstream defense than the tested unsupervised graph-anomaly baselines, while the supervised G-Safeguard comparison usefully illustrates the remaining performance gap.
Ablations provide evidence that neighborhood and global context contribute beyond individual response features. The paper is clearly organized and relevant to computational linguistics.
weaknesses: The central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. BlindGuard is described as defending against “any” or “entirely unknown” attack, but evaluation covers three non-adaptive attack families inherited from prior benchmarks. There is no adaptive attacker, coordinated attack study, subtle in-distribution attack, or attack designed to evade semantic-outlier detection.

The remediation specification appears technically inconsistent. The paper defines e_ij as communication from v_j to v_i, but Equation 8 and Algorithm 1 retain edges based on whether the receiving node is non-malicious. This removes traffic into detected attackers while apparently retaining their outgoing influence, contrary to the claimed bidirectional isolation. The discrepancy makes it unclear whether the evaluated implementation matches the method.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits essential information such as the exact SentenceBERT checkpoint, default agent count and number of attackers, graph construction details, dataset sizes and splits, normal-training-data construction, corruption fraction and intensity, temperature, training duration, threshold selection, random seeds, and baseline tuning. No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run statistics are reported, and the stated code-availability line provides no accessible link in the manuscript.

The defense assumes a fixed top-three anomaly budget. This effectively supplies knowledge about the number of agents to remove and can force benign-agent pruning when fewer than three agents are compromised. Sensitivity to the budget, unknown attack prevalence, threshold calibration, false-positive rates, and utility on completely benign systems are not evaluated.

Several empirical characterizations are inaccurate or unsupported. BlindGuard exceeds 80 AUC in only 10 of the 24 GPT-4o-mini settings in Table 1 and often trails G-Safeguard by large margins, so describing it as comparable to the supervised method “in most cases” is not justified. It also does not always achieve the best unsupervised ASR. Claims of significant superiority are made without statistical testing.

The methodological novelty is modest: the encoder concatenates individual features with one-hop and graph-wide means, while training uses Gaussian embedding corruption and a contrastive objective. The global mean does not substantiate the stronger claims about modeling long-range dependencies or coordinated malicious groups, neither of which is directly tested.

The scaling evidence is narrow, covering only PoisonRAG and comparing BlindGuard with no defense rather than with competing methods. Computational overhead, detection latency, API/token cost, and consequences of pruning for system connectivity are also absent despite the paper's practicality claims.

Overall, the results are promising, but the remediation ambiguity, missing protocol details, fixed attack-budget assumption, and overbroad generalization claims prevent a clear finding of soundness and reproducibility. Resolving these issues could make the work suitable for Findings.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical NLP-security problem: mitigating malicious-message propagation in LLM-based multi-agent systems without requiring labeled attacks.

BlindGuard is conceptually simple and computationally lightweight, combining frozen Sentence-BERT features, local and global graph context, contrastive representation learning, anomaly scoring, and graph pruning.

The empirical study is broad in surface coverage, spanning three attack modalities, four communication topologies, multiple LLM backbones, larger agent populations, collusion and adaptive attacks, and attack-free inputs.

BlindGuard generally improves detection AUC and downstream attack success rate over the evaluated unsupervised graph-anomaly baselines. The raw-Sentence-BERT and contextual-feature ablations provide some evidence that the learned hierarchical representation contributes beyond the frozen text encoder.
The paper acknowledges important failure modes, including benign reasoning diversity and on-topic, manifold-preserving attacks.
weaknesses: The remediation definition contains a central correctness ambiguity. With the paper's convention that e_ij is a message from v_j to v_i, Equation 8 retains an edge whenever receiver v_i is benign; it therefore leaves attacker-to-benign edges intact while removing only edges entering detected attackers. This contradicts the claimed bidirectional removal of all incident edges and appears again in Algorithm 1. The reported defense results cannot be interpreted confidently without resolving what was actually implemented.

The characterization of the synthetic corruption is internally inconsistent. Equation 5 samples normalized Gaussian noise, whose direction is isotropic and unrelated to message semantics or context. Nevertheless, the appendix claims the method does not rely on isotropic corruption and calls its negatives “semantics-aware” and targeted toward likely attack regions. No mechanism or analysis supports that claim; changing alpha changes magnitude, not directional isotropy.

The strongest claims—protection against “entirely unknown,” “universal,” and attack-agnostic threats—are substantially broader than the evidence. All evaluated attacks largely induce semantic output deviations, precisely the assumption built into the corruption objective. The adaptive experiment is only one manually designed prompt variant, and the failure analysis itself shows that on-topic adversarial steering can evade the detector.

The principal ASR evaluation assumes oracle knowledge that exactly three agents are compromised and always removes the top three. This is a strong deployment advantage and can make remediation effective even with modest ranking quality. The limited threshold experiment does not explain threshold calibration, report detection precision/recall or false-positive rates, or cover the full evaluation suite. AUC itself does not require knowledge of K, contrary to the experimental discussion.

Important experimental information is missing: numbers and construction of benign training graphs, train/validation/test separation, whether benign training queries overlap evaluation tasks, dataset sample sizes, corruption ratio, epochs, random seeds, variance or confidence intervals, attacked-node selection, random-topology generation, full prompts, and exact attack-success adjudication. The manuscript points only to the placeholder “Code,” so the contribution is not presently reproducible.

The evaluation lacks strong text-anomaly and one-class baselines trained on benign Sentence-BERT representations, such as centroid/density scoring, k-nearest-neighbor methods, isolation forests, or one-class objectives. Comparing primarily against generic graph-anomaly methods does not establish that the proposed contrastive construction is necessary. The raw-Sentence-BERT ablation is useful but insufficient.

The architectural novelty is modest: one-hop aggregation and a graph-wide mean are concatenated with frozen Sentence-BERT features and passed through an MLP, while inference uses average cosine dissimilarity. Claims about identifying coordinated groups and long-range dependencies are not directly established, particularly because every node receives the same global mean and attack prevalence is almost always fixed.

Several empirical conclusions overreach the presented data. The scalability table reports only ASR for one attack without detection quality, runtime scaling, baselines, or uncertainty; clean accuracy on a small apparent sample does not quantify the operational cost of falsely isolating benign agents; and many reported differences are too small to assess without repeated-run statistics. These validity and reproducibility issues require important revisions before a Findings recommendation is justified.

strengths: Addresses a relevant NLP-security problem: limiting malicious-message propagation in LLM-based multi-agent systems without requiring labeled attacks.

The proposed pipeline is straightforward and computationally lightweight, combining frozen SentenceBERT features, local/global graph summaries, contrastive training, anomaly ranking, and edge pruning.

The empirical study covers three attack families, four communication topologies, multiple LLM backbones, several graph-anomaly baselines, multi-round outcomes, clean inputs, and limited collusion/adaptive settings.
Reporting both detector AUC and downstream attack success rate is useful, and the appendix includes sensitivity, ablation, scalability, threshold, and failure-case analyses.
weaknesses: The central methodological justification is internally inconsistent. Equation 5 adds a normalized isotropic Gaussian vector, yet the paper later calls these samples "semantics-aware directional negatives" and explicitly denies relying on isotropic corruption. No mechanism directs corruption using semantics or context, and no evidence establishes that random off-manifold embedding noise resembles real malicious language.

The strongest claims exceed the results. In Table 1, BlindGuard attains AUC above 80 in fewer than half of the reported conditions and remains substantially below G-Safeguard in many cases, contrary to the text's "most cases" and broadly comparable-performance characterizations. Table 9 also does not show the claimed consistent superiority over raw SentenceBERT: the raw baseline has higher AUC for random-topology prompt injection and lower ASR for star-topology prompt injection.

The evaluation assumes exactly three compromised agents and generally supplies that true number to the top-K remediation rule. This is unrealistic and can materially inflate downstream defense performance. The threshold experiment is limited to two CSQA settings, does not explain calibration or score normalization, and therefore does not adequately validate unknown-prevalence deployment.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript gives no usable code link, training-set sizes or construction details, evaluation sample counts, random seeds, uncertainty estimates, corruption fraction, contrastive temperature, complete MLP architecture, decoding settings, or sufficient baseline-tuning details. Exact prompts and attack-generation procedures are largely deferred to prior work rather than specified.

The paper reports point estimates without repeated trials, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite stochastic LLM generation, synthetic corruption, and sometimes small numerical differences. This makes several comparative conclusions unreliable.

It is unclear whether detectors are retrained separately for every dataset, backbone, and topology or genuinely transferred across them. Consequently, the experiments do not substantiate the claimed "universal" or attack-agnostic generalization. The unseen-attack discussion is especially confusing because it describes a defense model as trained on prompt injection even though BlindGuard is said to use only benign data.

Baseline coverage is insufficient for isolating the contribution. Needed comparisons include one-class or density estimators over frozen embeddings, nearest-neighbor/Mahalanobis scoring, simple contextual-consistency detectors, random or centrality-based pruning, and stronger language-model-based safety judges. The raw-SBERT baseline appears only for two CSQA conditions.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed corruption and contrastive-learning choices: there is no comparison against ordinary Gaussian corruption, context-directed negatives, binary pseudo-label classification, alternative one-class objectives, or untrained/random encoders. Thus the claimed benefit of the main learning design remains unsupported.

The scalability evidence is weak: Table 3 compares only BlindGuard against no defense, changes prevalence by keeping three attackers as system size grows, omits detection quality and uncertainty, and tests only up to 50 agents despite quadratic pairwise scoring.

The adaptive attack is hand-designed and weak rather than optimized with knowledge of the detector; the paper itself acknowledges that on-topic, manifold-preserving attacks can evade the method. This substantially limits the claimed protection against unknown attacks.

The remediation definition is technically unclear: Equation 8 is described as bidirectional edge pruning but specifies only one endpoint condition, while edge-index conventions differ across equations and the algorithm. False-positive pruning can itself produce favorable ASR by disconnecting influential benign nodes, so detection and containment effects require more careful separation.

Overall, the idea is potentially repairable, but the unsupported corruption premise, overclaimed conclusions, oracle-like top-K setup, incomplete ablations, and missing reproducibility/statistical details prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the present form. A substantially revised paper could plausibly be ready for a subsequent review cycle.

strengths: Addresses an important and clearly NLP-relevant problem: limiting malicious information propagation in LLM-based multi-agent systems without requiring labeled examples of each attack type.

The proposed combination of frozen sentence representations, agent/neighborhood/system context, contrastive training with synthetic corruptions, anomaly scoring, and graph pruning is coherent and computationally lightweight.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering three attack modalities, multiple datasets, four communication topologies, several LLM backbones, larger agent populations, and multi-round outcomes. BlindGuard generally improves substantially over the unsupervised graph-anomaly baselines and often approaches the supervised baseline.

The paper includes useful supplementary analyses of encoder components, corruption intensity, collusion, a simple adaptive attack, attack-free task accuracy, and representative failure cases. The limitations concerning manifold-preserving attacks and benign reasoning diversity are candid and important.
The presentation is generally clear, with readable figures, formal definitions, an algorithm, and complexity analysis.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation assumes oracle knowledge of the number of compromised agents: every test case contains exactly three malicious agents and the defense selects exactly the top three. This conflicts with the claimed deployment setting of unknown attacks and guarantees unnecessary pruning when fewer or no attackers exist. The small threshold experiment does not resolve the issue because it reports task ASR rather than false-positive rate, number of agents pruned, calibration data, or robustness across attack prevalence and system size.

The corruption mechanism is mathematically isotropic normalized Gaussian noise, despite repeated descriptions such as “semantic-level,” “semantics-aware,” and “directional” negatives. Appendix H even states that the method does not rely on isotropic corruption, directly contradicting Eq. 5. No comparison against ordinary Gaussian noise, feature shuffling, text-level corruption, or context-directed hard negatives establishes that the claimed semantic simulation is responsible for the gains.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript does not specify core quantities such as train/validation/test sizes and splits, number of benign training graphs, corruption rate, number of epochs, random seeds, prompt templates, topology-generation parameters, or uncertainty across runs. The displayed code reference is merely “Code,” and the tables provide no confidence intervals or significance tests.

The generalization evidence is underspecified. It is unclear whether one detector is trained once and transferred across LLMs, datasets, topologies, and agent counts, or whether separate models are retrained on benign data for each condition. Consequently, claims of “universal” and attack-agnostic generalization are stronger than the documented protocol supports.

Several technical descriptions are inconsistent or incomplete. The purported hierarchical GNN is essentially one-hop normalized aggregation plus a graph-wide mean and an MLP; the global vector is identical for every node and does not itself model long-range agent-specific dependencies. The stated bidirectional pruning equation and Algorithm 1 appear to filter edges using only one endpoint, contrary to the prose. The supervised-contrastive objective also differs from the standard formulation without justification.

The experimental comparisons do not isolate whether gains arise from the proposed training objective, the hierarchical features, or simply contextual cosine scoring. The raw-SBERT and feature-removal ablations help, but missing objective-level ablations—binary classification, one-class objectives, no corruption, and matched corruption alternatives—leave the central methodological claim insufficiently supported.

The adaptive and collusion attacks are narrow, author-designed cases. Stronger white-box attacks that directly optimize contextual cosine similarity, manipulate several agents coherently, or preserve the benign semantic manifold are especially important because the paper's own failure analysis identifies these as the detector's central vulnerability.
